query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of Al to equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will improve its oxygen resistance by forming a protective alumina-based oxide scale, with minimal impact on mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy exhibiting 8–16% room-temperature ductility and 163–530 MPa yield strength at 1000 °C but poor oxidation resistance.
generation.intervention: Vacuum arc melt HfNbTaTiZr with a small Al addition (e.g., 2–5 at%), targeting the formation of a stable Al-containing oxide scale.
generation.conditions: Perform isothermal oxidation tests at 800–1000 °C in air for 5–100 h under tensile loading up to strain rates of 10−2 s−1.
generation.structural_mediator: In situ formation of an Al-rich oxide layer at high temperatures that impedes oxygen ingress.
generation.mechanism: The added Al promotes the nucleation of a continuous, dense alumina-based layer which suppresses the rapid inward diffusion of oxygen, thereby mitigating the pest-like oxidation and preserving the alloy's bulk properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Mass gain from oxidation will be significantly reduced (e.g., by more than half) compared with the Al-free alloy, while room- and high-temperature tensile properties remain comparable to the baseline HfNbTaTiZr.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr cast alloy exhibits suboptimal oxidation resistance, leading to embrittlement and surface degradation at elevated temperatures in air.
generation.boundary: Applicable for high-temperature service up to approximately 1000 °C in air, under moderate strains (up to ~10–15%) over test durations of up to 100 h.
generation.uncertainty: Exact optimum Al composition and the long-term stability of the oxide scale require further investigation, and mechanical property trade-offs at higher Al contents remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct side-by-side isothermal oxidation tests of unmodified and Al-doped HfNbTaTiZr samples exposed at 800 and 1000 °C in air for 5–100 h under nominal tensile stress (e.g., 50% of baseline yield strength). Measure mass gain and post-test ductility.
measurements: Mass change (oxide scale growth) using thermogravimetric analysis
Microstructural and compositional analysis of oxide layers (SEM/EDS/XRD)
Residual tensile ductility after thermal exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-doped alloy does not exhibit a significantly reduced mass gain (less than ~50% of the baseline) or loses a similar or greater fraction of its tensile ductility compared to the undoped control, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractAlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) films with strong amorphization were obtained by co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition, and the effect of thermal shock on the films was investigated in order to explore the protection mechanism of HEA films against mechanical components in extreme service environments. The results show that after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing, so that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film exhibits excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air. In the friction-corrosion coupling environment, the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C for 1 h shows the best tribocorrosion resistance due to the stable dense microstructure and excellent mechanical properties, and its ΔOCP, COF and wear rate possess the smallest values of 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1.Keywords: AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film, thermal shock, oxidation, tribocorrosion

Structural metallic materials for applications at high temperatures must have a balance of mechanical properties and oxidation resistance. Coated and internally cooled Ni-based superalloys are used in gas turbine engines close to their high temperature limit, which is imposed by the melting temperature of Ni. The search for new alloys with similar or better capabilities at higher temperatures has concentrated on Nb-silicide based alloys that have lower densities, significantly higher solidus temperatures in excess of 1900 °C and can offer notable mechanical properties []. For example, some of these alloys can have compressive yield strength of about 1800 MPa at room temperature, 1200 MPa at 1000 °C and 500 MPa at 1200 °C []. The oxidation resistance of Nb-silicide based alloys was improved dramatically when the key alloying elements Al, Cr, Si, and Ti were in synergy with other transition and refractory metals, for example Hf, Mo, and simple metal and metalloid elements, e.g., Sn [,,,,]. The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add an element which interacts frequently with the alloy, such as Mo.
